The IEEE 802.11 standard identifies three elements:

  • Access Point (AP): controls an area called a Basic Service Set (BSS) and provides access to the distribution system.
  • Wireless terminals: they connect to the Access Point.
  • Distribution system: generally, the wired LAN.

Since there is an Access Point, this is called infrastructure mode (there is another variant, ad-hoc, without APs). We focus on the data link layer: how frames travel between the terminals and the AP.
Infrastructure mode = terminals + an Access Point that links them to the wired LAN.
The same layer model, a different MAC

In the wired LAN the data link layer had two sublayers: LLC on top and another that depended on the technology. In Wireless LAN it is the same:

  • Upper sublayer: the 802.2 standard (LLC), the same as Ethernet.
  • Lower sublayer: 802.11 MAC, which defines how the wireless medium is accessed.

Below is the physical layer, which here is radio.
Nothing changes for the upper layers: what gets replaced is the MAC sublayer (and the physical layer).

The radio spectrum is regulated: each device is assigned a frequency band. Wireless LAN operates in the 2.4 GHz band, split into 11 channels of 22 MHz.

The problem is that the channels overlap: each one shares frequencies with its neighbors.

Only three do not overlap with each other: 1, 6 and 11. That is why devices in this band generally operate on those three channels.
In 2.4 GHz there are 11 channels, but only 3 that do not interfere: 1, 6 and 11.
Each row shows channels that do not overlap with each other (frequencies in MHz)

The 5 GHz band is wider than the previous one: it has more channels and they do not overlap.

In addition, the technologies that use this band allow bonding neighboring channels to form a wider channel. More bandwidth means more transmission speed.
More spectrum, separate channels and the option to combine them: that is why 5 GHz performs better.

Communication in this network is always from the terminal to the Access Point or vice versa. A terminal does not talk directly to another terminal: it hands the frame to the AP and the AP forwards it.

That is why we say it is a centralized medium access control.

Important consequence: each terminal needs visibility to the Access Point, but not to the rest of the devices.
To and from the Access Point: never terminal to terminal.
Why CSMA/CD does not work: the hidden node

On the LAN we used CSMA/CD: listening to the medium before transmitting. In wireless that is not practical.

Two terminals can see the AP but not see each other, for example with an obstacle in between. Neither can know whether the other is transmitting: this is the hidden node.

That is why CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance) is used: the goal is to avoid collisions, because the cost of recovering from them is very high.
CD = detect the collision and recover. CA = do whatever possible so it doesn't happen.
DCF with RTS / CTS: asking permission

It was the original control algorithm, designed for the hidden node. The sender is the terminal and the destination is the Access Point.

  • The station listens to the medium (as far as it can hear): it must be idle for a DIFS interval.
  • It sends an RTS (Request To Send).
  • The AP answers with a CTS (Clear To Send): it may transmit.

B may not have heard the RTS, but it does hear the CTS, because it has visibility to the AP. So it sets a virtual carrier: the NAV.
The CTS comes from the AP, and everyone hears the AP: that is how hidden nodes find out too.
Data, ACK and the others' NAV

After the CTS, the sender transmits the data. The AP confirms with an ACK if it received them correctly: there may be interference, with so many devices in the band.

The NAV is a virtual carrier: whoever hears an RTS or a CTS sets it for the time that frame indicates. While it is set, the station knows another terminal is transmitting and does not interfere.

When the ACK is detected, the NAV is cleared. The stations wait a DIFS and try to win the channel.
NAV (RTS) if I heard the request, NAV (CTS) if I heard the reply: either way, I stay quiet.
Basic DCF: no RTS or CTS

It was noticed that the hidden node was not so common, and the mechanism changed. A station with something to transmit:

  • Checks its NAV. If it is set, it waits and runs the exponential backoff (the one from LAN networks).
  • If it is clear, it listens to the medium. If idle for a DIFS, it transmits.
  • If it receives the ACK, it transmitted successfully. If not, there was a collision: backoff before retransmitting.
Here the collision is not detected by listening: it is inferred because the ACK did not arrive.

• Infrastructure mode: everything goes through the Access Point.
  • 2.4 GHz: channels 1, 6 and 11. 5 GHz: more channels, no overlap.
  • Hidden node: CSMA/CD does not work; collisions are avoided (CSMA/CA).
  • DIFS → RTS → CTS → data → ACK, with the NAV silencing the rest.
  • Basic DCF: NAV, DIFS, transmit and wait for the ACK; if it doesn't arrive, backoff.

With or without RTS/CTS there is randomness: a station never knows how long it will wait. Synchronous applications need some certainty: that is why PCF was invented, the topic of the next lesson.
Why are channels 1, 6 and 11 almost always used in 2.4 GHz?
Because they have the highest power
Because they are the only three that do not overlap with each other
Because the others are reserved for the Access Point
Because they are the only 22 MHz ones
There are 11 channels of 22 MHz that overlap with their neighbors; only 1, 6 and 11 do not share frequencies.
What is the hidden node problem?
A terminal that cannot see the Access Point
An Access Point that is not in the list of networks
Two terminals that see the AP but cannot hear each other
A terminal that transmits without waiting for the DIFS
Each terminal needs visibility to the AP, not to the others; if two cannot hear each other, neither knows when the other transmits.
A terminal did not hear the RTS, but did hear the Access Point's CTS. What does it do?
It transmits, because the CTS gives it permission
It sets its NAV for the time the CTS indicates and does not transmit
It immediately sends its own RTS
The CTS tells it another terminal is going to transmit: it sets the virtual carrier (NAV) and waits until it is cleared.
In basic DCF, how does a station know its frame collided?
Because it compares what it hears with what it transmits
Because the AP sends it a jam
If the ACK arrives it transmitted correctly; if not, there was a collision and it runs the exponential backoff before retransmitting.
Access Point + terminals + distribution system (the wired LAN). The area the AP controls is the BSS.
